item.title: Learning unknown stabilizer codes using product measurements
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Stabilizer generators of an unknown stabilizer code can be reconstructed from N≥Aln⁡g+Aln⁡(1/δ) states using single-qubit product measurements, requiring polylogarithmically many copies in physical qubit count n for qLDPC codes.

Grade 0.491 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Heather Leitch, Sowmya Tirukkovalluri, Yingkai Ouyang

Figure

Step-by-step schematic for measuring random bases on N codewords, recording bit outcomes, evaluating subset parities, and filtering stabilizer generators via thresholding.

Asks

Can stabilizer generators of an unknown quantum error-correcting code be learned using only local single-qubit measurements on codewords without prior structural knowledge?

But

Bounded stabilizer generator weight w, code defined in stabilizer formalism, failure probability δ, bit-flip error rate per qubit p.

Tools

randomized product Pauli measurements · parity checks on qubit subsets · multiplicative Chernoff bounds

Abstract

Efficiently characterizing quantum error correcting codes is a key challenge on the path to fault-tolerant quantum computation. Stabilizer codes, a central class of such codes, are defined by a set of stabilizer generators. Here, we present an algorithm that uses random single-qubit measurements to learn the stabilizer generators of any stabilizer code from N copies of stabilizer states in its codespace, requiring no prior knowledge of the code's structure. This also enables verification that a device implements its intended code. We derive a lower bound on N needed to recover the stabilizer generators with high probability, together with a bound on the algorithm's overall probability of success. When applied to quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, a leading candidate for practical fault-tolerant architectures, our approach requires a number of states that scales polylogarithmically with n, the number of qubits.

item.title: Efficient Quantum Error Correction from Three Dimensional Qubit Control
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — 3D neutral-atom embedding of the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code achieves approximately 4× higher areal logical-qubit density than planar layout and 42× higher than distance-11 surface codes, while halving syndrome-extraction round duration.

Grade 0.486 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Kevin Yipu Wu, Ohik Kwon, Maxwell F. Parsons

Figure

Syndrome-extraction round cycle time broken down by operation (readout, transport, transfer, and gates) across surface-code, systolic planar, LR-planar, and LR-triangular 3D architectures, showing total time halved in 3D relative to the planar baseline.

Asks

How does native 3D qubit control affect the routing overhead, footprint, and temporal execution cost of nonlocal qLDPC syndrome extraction?

Before

Planar 2D atom-array embeddings of the [[144,12,12]] code.

But

Numerical simulation rather than physical hardware implementation. Assumes single-shot multi-layer readout and collision-free parallel 3D transport.

Tools

3D optical tweezer arrays · Rydberg blockade routing · Bivariate bicycle code · Collective check-register transport scheduling

Abstract

High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can substantially reduce qubit overhead relative to surface codes, but their advantage depends on efficiently realizing nonlocal syndrome extraction. We study the \([[144,12,12]]\) bivariate bicycle code on a neutral-atom architecture with native three-dimensional (3D) geometry, comparing planar and 3D embeddings while holding the code fixed. We characterize spatial efficiency using the logical-qubit density, defined as the number of encoded logical qubits per unit spatial footprint. Because the optical controller's field of view limits the transverse extent of an array, this metric estimates the number of logical qubits that can be accommodated within a fixed optical field of view. The 3D embedding achieves approximately \(4×\) greater areal logical-qubit density than the planar layout and \(42×\) greater than a surface-code baseline. It also reduces the bivariate bicycle syndrome-extraction time by roughly \(2×\) compared to a planar baseline, with fewer movement operations and substantially shorter atom-transport distance. Native 3D geometry can improve both the packing density and executable realization of nonlocal qLDPC codes, making practical performance depend jointly on code structure, optical geometry, transport scheduling, and hardware-level noise. This motivates further development of control techniques in 3D.

item.title: TETRIS-Q: Tiling-based Effective Transient-fault Reduction on Interleaved Superconducting Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Combining substrate phonon barrier tiling with QEC interleaving reduces peak logical error rate by over 99.8% and shortens transient duration by 80% under simulated radiation strikes. Sparser multi-qubit tiling cuts barrier fabrication perimeter cost by up to 87% with minimal performance loss.

Grade 0.440 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Marzio Vallero, Gioele Casagranda, Flavio Vella, Paolo Rech

Figure

Heatmap of average logical error rate for a distance-7 rotated surface code across tile sizes (1 to 16 qubits) and numbers of interleaved codes (1 to 9) at barrier permeability bp=0.1.

Asks

Can substrate-level phonon barrier tiling and quantum error correction code interleaving mitigate radiation-induced spatially correlated faults in superconducting quantum chips without execution overhead?

But

Numerical simulation only (51 million circuit simulations) using rotated surface codes under a parametrizable barrier permeability model (bp).

Tools

TETRIS-Q planar-mesh tiling algorithm · rotated surface code simulation · substrate-level phonon barrier model · QEC code interleaving

Abstract

The struggle of the hour in quantum computing research is achieving effective suppression of the error mechanisms induced by the interaction of external radiation with superconducting quantum devices. Despite the rapid advancements in quantum error correction (QEC) of recent years, radiation-induced faults are yet to be fully addressed. These events are known to be the cause of simultaneous correlated defects in qubits that lie onto a single substrate, ultimately jeopardising QEC code effectiveness. In this paper, we propose to selectively combine substrate-level phonon barriers and QEC interleaving via a planar-mesh tiling algorithm, TETRIS-Q, reaching efficient and effective suppression of radiation events. Our cross-layer solution comes at no extra cost in terms of QEC code execution or decoding time. We model and simulate radiation-induced transient faults over a plethora of barrier and QEC interleaving configurations. Through more than 51 million quantum circuit simulations, we show peak logical error reductions of more than 99.8 %, together with an 80% reduction of the observable transient duration with permeable barriers. We find that sparser tiling can reach comparable performance to single qubit tiling, prompting cost reductions of upwards of 87 % in barrier tracing. By leveraging independent QEC code interleaving, we measure up to one order of magnitude average logical error rate reductions without the use of permeable barriers, and up to three orders of magnitude with the joint usage of barriers.

item.title: Compiling the 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation algorithm for active volume quantum architectures
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Active-volume-aware compilation cuts the active volume of 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy estimation by up to 3.9× across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20. Also cuts Toffoli count by ∼2× at L=20.

Grade 0.422 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Harriet Apel, Athena Caesura, Carys Harvey, Sam Heavey, Angus Kan, Jessica Lemieux, Ryan Levy, Sam Pallister, Joseph Peetz, William Pol, Sukin Sim, William A. Simon, Mark Steudtner, Gideon Uchehara

Figure

Active volume and conventional computational spacetime volume plotted against logical qubit count across square lattice sizes L=4 to 20, comparing baseline against improved compilation.

Asks

How much can the execution cost and runtime of quantum phase estimation for 2D Fermi-Hubbard ground-state energy be reduced by compiling directly for active-volume architectures instead of non-Clifford proxies?

Before

Baseline compilation optimized for non-Clifford cost, as analyzed by Campbell (2022) and Kan et al. (2024).

But

Evaluated for t=1, u=8 with periodic boundary conditions and extensive energy error budget 0.0051tLxLy.

Tools

active-volume-aware compilation · second-order Suzuki-Trotter evolution · sine-window quantum phase estimation · batched Hamming weight phasing · oriented ZX calculus

Abstract

As quantum computing enters the early fault-tolerant era, circuit compilation choices will increasingly depend on details of the underlying architecture rather than solely optimizing for generic proxies such as non-Clifford count. We present an active-volume-aware compilation of the ground-state energy estimation algorithm for the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model using quantum phase estimation and Trotterized time evolution. The proposed compilation reduces the active volume across L×L square lattices with L=4 to 20, achieving up to a 3.9× reduction over prior work optimized for non-Clifford cost. As a by-product of these compilation improvements, the resulting circuits also achieve state-of-the-art Toffoli counts, with a ~2× reduction for the L=20 case. Lastly, the active volume architecture and recent execution scheduling advances provide a means of translating these reduction trends into runtime. This demonstrates the increasing importance of architecture-aware compilation for practical early fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: DPRQ: A Dynamic Programming-based Qubit Routing Algorithm for Collective Communication in Distributed Quantum Computing
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Dynamic programming qubit routing reduces inter-node EPR pair consumption by an average of 24.40% and up to 85.06% across 80 circuit configurations.

Grade 0.410 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Dhaval Vaidya (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA), Ruozhou Yu (North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA)

Figure

EPR cost plotted against total circuit qubits (50 to 200) for DPRQ versus QuComm across four benchmark circuits. DPRQ maintains lower communication cost as network size increases.

Asks

How to minimize inter-node communication across collective communication blocks in distributed quantum circuits by accounting for global inter-block dependencies?

Before

QuComm compiler, which uses greedy block-level routing.

But

Evaluated on 4 benchmark circuits (QAOA, RCA, BV, VQE) up to 200 qubits in simulation across 3 network topologies (mesh-grid, ring, fully-connected).

Tools

dynamic programming · collective quantum communication · TP-Comm protocol · communication fusion · shortest-path early execution

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing (DQC) offers a promising approach to scale quantum computing by overcoming the resource limitations of a single quantum processor. However, inter-node communication remains a major bottleneck of DQC due to inefficient and error-prone entanglement distribution. Optimizing inter-node communication can not only reduce the amount of entanglement resource needed to execute a quantum circuit but also improve execution speed and accuracy of the results. This paper proposes DPRQ, a qubit routing algorithm for minimizing inter-node communication in distributed quantum circuits divided into collective communication blocks. Unlike current approaches that utilize greedy block-level qubit routing strategies, DPRQ employs a dynamic programming-based technique focused on global circuit-level optimization, while capturing inter-block dependencies. We evaluated DPRQ on four sets of quantum circuits and a variety of DQC configurations. The results demonstrate that DPRQ's innovative routing strategy achieves an average of 24.40% reduction with a maximum of 85.06% reduction in inter-node communication, when compared to the state-of-the-art collective communication-based DQC compiler QuComm.

item.title: Thermal lifetime of the centralized repetition code: From quantum annealing to social dynamics
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Centralized repetition code storage lifetime scales exponentially with qubit count n at any finite temperature T<∞, avoiding the thermal instability of a 1D Ising chain despite having only 1 Ising bond per qubit.

Grade 0.406 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Ari Mizel, Van Molino

Figure

Upper bound on the transition rate eigenvalue λ1 plotted against qubit number n at inverse temperature βJ=0.8. The decay toward zero illustrates exponentially increasing stability with system size even when thermal energy kBT exceeds coupling J.

Asks

Does a star-graph centralized repetition code behave thermodynamically like an unstable 1D Ising chain or a stable complete-graph repetition code under thermal noise?

But

Local bit-flip error model only (does not suppress phase errors). Assumes Born-Markov bath coupling and odd physical qubit number n.

Tools

Lindblad master equation · spectral analysis · variational eigenvalue bounds · Gershgorin circle theorem

Abstract

There is an extensive body of research probing the potential of adiabatic quantum computation and quantum annealing to solve hard computational problems. This research endeavor is complicated by noise afflicting hardware during the computational process. An error-correcting approach called quantum annealing correction (QAC) was suggested to mitigate this noise. The QAC approach employs a centralized version of the repetition code in which the qubits are configured in a star-graph pattern with one special qubit playing the role of the hub. In this paper, we explore the thermal physics of the centralized repetition code, using a Lindblad equation framework to analyze its lifetime when coupled to a thermal bath. We show that its centralized configuration leads to thermal stability, enabling the robust storage of a logical bit of information, despite the fact that there is only 1 ferromagnetic Ising interaction per qubit like a 1-dimensional Ising chain.
